title: Build Versus Buy and Return on Investment
subtitle: Compare ownership costs, not only invoices
summary: Pip compares an observability invoice with a “free” internal stack. Maintenance and displaced product work change the calculation. Both options need a common horizon, required investigative outcomes, and honest assumptions about adoption, integration, and recurring effort.

concepts.title: Total ownership includes ongoing work
concepts.body: Pip calls the market’s observability stack free while three engineers maintain it. Ownership includes infrastructure, hiring, upgrades, incidents, integration, and support as well as software price. Open source can still be the right choice. Pip counts employee time so an invisible labor cost is not compared unfairly with a visible invoice.

concepts.title: Opportunity cost changes the comparison
concepts.body: Pip spends a quarter building query infrastructure and delays a customer feature. Engineering time has an alternative use. Forgone product and reliability improvements belong in the build-versus-buy comparison, especially when tooling is not the business’s product. Pip asks which choice preserves capacity for core goals, not only which invoice is smaller.

concepts.title: An internal platform is a product
concepts.body: Pip’s fast internal backend attracts few investigators. Requirements, usable workflows, prioritization, support, and adoption are product responsibilities. Custom integration and expertise can justify building, but storage and queries alone do not fund those duties. Pip fixes undocumented investigation workarounds rather than treating technical feasibility as product success.

concepts.title: Compare benefits on a common horizon
concepts.body: Pip compares a monthly invoice with a one-time prototype and rejects the mismatch. Both options need the same horizon and required outcomes. Buying may deliver useful investigation sooner; building may provide locally important fit or control. Pip separates initial, recurring, migration, and integration costs, recording assumptions for later reassessment.

misconceptions.claim: Open-source software has no ongoing ownership cost.
misconceptions.correction: Licensing can be free while infrastructure, staffing, integration, and operational work remain substantial.

misconceptions.claim: Building a working backend proves the build option is successful.
misconceptions.correction: The platform must also deliver usable workflows and sustained adoption for its internal users.

scenario.title: The invisible platform team
scenario.context: A commercial quote looks expensive, but an internal stack already occupies several engineers.

options.label: Compare full ownership and displaced work
options.benefit: Makes staffing, operations, and product delay visible.
options.cost: Requires gathering costs across multiple budgets.
options.consequence: Decision makers can see which option preserves more capacity for business priorities.

options.label: Choose solely by the license line
options.benefit: Is quick and aligns with the visible purchasing budget.
options.cost: Can select the more expensive option by omitting hidden work.
options.consequence: The internal stack can win on paper while consuming more total resources.

scenario.debrief: Compare the same outcome and time horizon, with costs included wherever the organization currently records them.

quiz.question: Which comparison is most misleading?
options: Annual ownership costs for both options
A vendor invoice against infrastructure plus staff and support
A vendor invoice against an internal stack labeled free
quiz.explanation: Existing staffing and infrastructure remain real costs even when they sit outside the software budget.

quiz.question: Why include opportunity cost?
options: The same engineering time could produce value elsewhere
A quoted license price already accounts for all forgone engineering work
Existing staff time is a sunk cost and should be excluded from either option
quiz.explanation: The value of displaced work is part of choosing how to allocate scarce engineering effort.

quiz.question: What risk remains after an internal backend meets performance targets?
options: Performance targets determine whether internal users will adopt the workflow
Its workflows may still fail to attract effective adoption
A working prototype removes the need for ongoing product prioritization
quiz.explanation: Usability and internal product management matter alongside technical performance.
